content:
Actor Andrew Scott has emerged as a top contender on many awards season forecasts after delivering a heart-wrenching performance in “Elsinore,” a new biographical drama.

The film —written by Stephen Beresford and directed by Simon Stone — follows Scottish actor Ian Charleson (played by Scott) as he gears up to tackle the title role in “Hamlet” on the London stage in 1989.

Charleson is gay and, unbeknownst to many of his co-stars, HIV positive. Just before rehearsals for “Hamlet” get underway, he learns he is dying of an AIDS-related illness, meaning the role will be his last.

In an interview with HuffPost shortly before “Elsinore” premiered in New York last week, Beresford acknowledged he had Scott in mind to play Charleson from the get-go.

“I wrote it for him, really, with his voice in my head,” he explained, while noting he’s hopeful viewers will see Charleson’s story as a “life-affirming” example of “resilience in the face of crisis.”

To modern audiences, Charleson is best remembered for the 1981 movie “Chariots of Fire,” a point which “Elsinore” acknowledges with humor. As the film also shows, the actor’s “Hamlet” was a critical smash. Sadly, his health declined during the play’s run, and he died in January 1990 at age 40, becoming the first celebrity death in the U.K. publicly attributed to HIV/AIDS.

Fleshing out the screenplay gave Beresford an opportunity to interview many of Charleson’s friends and acquaintances, including Dr. Margaret Johnson (played by two-time Oscar winner Olivia Colman in the film), the pioneering physician who oversaw Charleson’s care in the final months of his life, and “Hamlet” director Richard Eyre (Johnny Flynn).

“In the British theater, the story of Ian playing Hamlet is legendary, but like a lot of legends, it gets talked about in very simple terms,” Beresford said. “I was drawn to the fact that it’s a story about a man who is publicly closeted, and normally in stories like that, the redemptive moment is coming out. That isn’t what happens for Ian at all. So I wanted to dig into that ... how do I make that the hero’s journey, as it were?”

Beresford’s most striking revelation came from Eyre, who shared details about a phone conversation he had with Charleson just days before the actor’s death. At the time, Eyre recalled, Charleson was energized by the success of “Hamlet,” and had mapped out his plans to take on other Shakespearean roles, including “King Lear” and Benedict in “Much Ado About Nothing.”

“Elsinore” makes that ambitious drive apparent in a key scene where Charleson and a fellow patient, Nicholas (Joe Locke), choreograph a group dance number set to a disco version of Ethel Merman’s “There’s No Business Like Show Business” in their hospital ward.

The scene, Beresford said, is a wink at Charleson’s own impressions of Merman, as corroborated by several of the late actor’s friends.

The screenwriter also drew from a conversation he’d had with one of the lead producers of Andrew Lloyd Webber’s “Cats,” who recalled many of the musical’s performers being hospitalized with AIDS in the early 1980s.

“The crossover between artists in the theater and the AIDS crisis was incredibly strong, especially at the beginning,” he said. “However, we did live through it, and we did dance and we did laugh.”

Scott, who rose to prominence in the U.S. as the “Hot Priest” of “Fleabag,” is a former Hamlet in his own right. If he receives an Academy Award nomination for “Elsinore,” as is widely expected, he could be on the path to making history as the first openly gay man to win an Oscar for Best Actor.

For many of Scott’s fans, it’ll be an overdue honor, as the actor’s lack of an Academy Award nomination for his performance in the 2023 romantic drama “All of Us Strangers” was considered a snub.

Beresford, whose credits include the 2012 play “The Last of the Haussmans” and the 2014 film “Pride,” is keeping mum on the awards buzz as the film opens across the U.S. over Thanksgiving and in early December.

“No prizes, no punishments,” he quipped, citing the advice of a childhood teacher. “I try not to think about it [but] I love Andrew and he is family to me, so I find it incredibly moving that we’re here now at last.”

“I feel very strongly about sharing our history with younger generations, because it’s been silenced or sidelined,” he added. “One of the messages of ‘Elsinore’ is about our resilience, and being able to say, ‘This is the heritage that you come from.’ We are very strong and we’ve always been here and we always will be.’ To share in that, I think, can be very enriching.”
